Life of a Quant 📈📉

Years of math, Python, C++, stochastic calculus, Monte Carlo... and then the vibe quanting era shows up. 😅

Vibe coding: the good and the bad

✅ Pros

• Prototypes in minutes, not days

• Lower barrier for non-programmers

• Less boilerplate and repetitive code

• Cheap, fast experiments

• Great for learning

⚠️ Cons

• Hidden bugs (in quant work, one subtle error can fake your profits)

• Security risks if nobody reviews the code

• Your fundamentals can fade

• Hard to maintain code you don't understand

• Overconfidence in output that only looks right

My take: use AI as an assistant, but review, test and understand what it writes.

title: Your portfolio is "diversified"... until the market crashes. 📉
trading_type: Options Trading, Quantitative & Algorithmic, Risk Management
cleaned_caption:
Your portfolio is "diversified"... until the market crashes. 📉

Normal days: each sector moves on its own.

Average ρ ≈ 0.2 → portfolio risk 12%

Crisis: they all fall together.

Average ρ → 0.9 → portfolio risk 19%

Same portfolio. Same weights. 60% more risk.

σₚ = σ√(1/n + (1−1/n)ρ̄)

Why does this happen? 🧠

In a one-factor model, ρᵢⱼ ≈ βᵢβⱼσ²ₘ/(σᵢσⱼ).

When market volatility σₘ spikes, the common factor swamps each sector's own risk, so correlations rise mechanically.

For the quants 🤓

• Correlation measured in high-vol regimes is biased upward (Forbes & Rigobon, 2002)

• Real crises spike σ too, so actual risk rises even more than shown

• Hedges cost money: puts bleed premium in calm markets

We saw it in 2008. We saw it in March 2020.

Diversify for normal days. Hedge for crisis days. 🛡️

title: Most people think gamma scalping is "buy low, sell high."
cleaned_caption:
Most people think gamma scalping is "buy low, sell high."

Quants know it's a bet on one thing: realized vol vs implied vol. ⚡

1️⃣ Θ = −½ΓS²σᵢ² → theta IS the price of gamma (16% vol ≈ 1% daily breakeven)

2️⃣ Daily P&L ≈ ½ΓS²[(ΔS/S)² − σᵢ²Δt]

3️⃣ Path dependence → vol near the strike pays most (dollar gamma weighting)

4️⃣ Hedge at implied vs realized vol → smooth path or locked total (Ahmad–Wilmott)

5️⃣ Discrete hedging error ∝ 1/√N (Derman–Kamal)

6️⃣ With costs, hedge in a band, not at a point (Whalley–Wilmott)

7️⃣ IV > RV on average → long gamma is negative carry

8️⃣ BS delta ignores the smile → use skew-aware delta

The edge isn't the hedge. It's forecasting realized vol better than the market. 📈

title: How do HFT firms trade in nanoseconds? ⚡
cleaned_caption:
How do HFT firms trade in nanoseconds? ⚡

1️⃣ FIX → the universal text protocol (35=D = NewOrderSingle)

2️⃣ Native Binary → each exchange's own fast protocol (BOE, OUCH)

3️⃣ SBE → fixed-layout binary behind CME MDP 3.0 & iLink 3

4️⃣ ITCH → Nasdaq's feed of every order book event

5️⃣ UDP Multicast → one packet, thousands of receivers (A/B feeds for gaps)

6️⃣ Colocation → your servers inside the exchange data center

7️⃣ Kernel Bypass → skip the OS, NIC straight to your app (DPDK, Onload)

8️⃣ FPGA → parsing + risk checks in hardware, sub-microsecond

The edge isn't just the strategy. It's the plumbing. 🔧

title: Alpha isn't found in one skill. It's built at the intersection of
cleaned_caption:
Alpha isn't found in one skill. It's built at the intersection of several. 🧠📈

What does it take to develop a real quantitative trading strategy?

🧮 Math & Statistics — Understand probability, regression, and uncertainty.

💻 ML & Code — Turn hypotheses into models, features, and executable systems.

📊 Market Microstructure — Understand liquidity, execution, transaction costs, and how markets actually behave.

🎯 Quant Alpha — Find a statistical edge that survives out-of-sample testing and can scale under real-world constraints.

But here's the part many overlook:

A strategy that performs well in a backtest isn't necessarily an edge.

Your signal must survive:

• Transaction costs

• Overfitting

• Market regime changes

• Execution constraints

• Out-of-sample validation

The goal isn't to build the most complex model. It's to find a robust, repeatable edge.
